title: Saudi air defense running low
ticker: BREAKING: Saudi Arabia running low on missile interceptors after Houthi strikes
Missile strike on Riyadh airport kills 13, wounds about 300
Saudi Arabia asked France, Britain, Pakistan and Egypt for air defense support
Pakistan confirms its forces are in the kingdom under the Makkah defense pact
Trump weighs joining the fight against the Houthis

lines.speaker: Anchor
lines.text: Good evening, and welcome to KOWEN News.

lines.speaker: Anchor
lines.text: Saudi Arabia, one of the world's biggest military spenders, is reportedly *running low* on the missiles it needs to shoot down incoming attacks.

lines.speaker: Anchor
lines.text: A Houthi missile has hit *Riyadh's main airport*, killing thirteen people.

lines.speaker: Anchor
lines.text: And the kingdom has turned to its allies, including *Pakistan*, for help.

lines.speaker: Anchor
lines.text: Tonight: the attack, why the kingdom's shield is wearing thin, who is coming to help, and whether *America* could be pulled in.

lines.speaker: Anchor
lines.text: Here's what's happening.

lines.speaker: Reporter
lines.text: On Saturday, a missile struck a passenger terminal at *King Khalid International Airport* in Riyadh.

lines.speaker: Reporter
lines.text: Saudi authorities said twelve people were killed and around *three hundred* wounded, some critically.

lines.speaker: Reporter
lines.text: India's embassy later said one of its citizens had died of his injuries, bringing the toll to *thirteen*.

lines.speaker: Reporter
lines.text: It was the *deadliest attack* on a Gulf Arab nation since the Iran war began.

lines.speaker: Reporter
lines.text: Yemen's Iran backed *Houthi rebels* claimed responsibility.

lines.speaker: Reporter
lines.text: The next day, another projectile hit the same airport complex, killing one more person and injuring eleven. The airport in *Dammam* was also attacked.

lines.speaker: Reporter
lines.text: Saudi Arabia defends itself mainly with American made systems, including *Patriot* and *THAAD* missile batteries.

lines.speaker: Reporter
lines.text: Every incoming missile or drone can require one or more expensive *interceptor missiles* to stop it.

lines.speaker: Reporter
lines.text: And according to Saudi officials cited by the Wall Street Journal, the kingdom is *running low* on those interceptors.

lines.speaker: Reporter
lines.text: Officials say Saudi Arabia has been moving batteries around to protect *palaces* and *energy infrastructure*.

lines.speaker: Reporter
lines.text: Even successful interceptions carry risks. Debris from one intercepted ballistic missile reportedly hit a *kindergarten* and a medical clinic complex.

lines.speaker: Reporter
lines.text: The United States has also seen its own interceptor stockpile *dwindle* during the war with Iran.

lines.speaker: Reporter
lines.text: Last month, regional officials told the Associated Press that Saudi Arabia had asked four countries to deploy *air defense support*.

lines.speaker: Reporter
lines.text: France, Britain, *Pakistan*, and Egypt.

lines.speaker: Reporter
lines.text: Money is not the problem. Saudi Arabia spent an estimated *eighty three billion dollars* on its military last year, the eighth most in the world.

lines.speaker: Reporter
lines.text: The problem is *time*. Interceptors must be built, shipped and installed, and factories can't make them overnight.

lines.speaker: Anchor
lines.text: One ally has already answered: *Pakistan*.

lines.speaker: Reporter
lines.text: On August seventh, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkiye signed the *Makkah Joint Defense Agreement*.

lines.speaker: Reporter
lines.text: It commits the three countries to treat an armed attack on one as *an attack on all*.

lines.speaker: Reporter
lines.text: On October fifth, at a meeting in Riyadh, the three allies agreed to provide *designated forces* and military capabilities under the pact.

lines.speaker: Reporter
lines.text: Turkiye is also sending mainly *defensive and technical* support, according to Reuters.

lines.speaker: Reporter
lines.text: Turkiye has *NATO's second largest army*. Together with Pakistan, it has condemned the Houthi attacks and agreed to join a Saudi-led coalition to protect shipping in the Red Sea.

scenes.name: Lt. Gen. Ahmed Sharif Chaudhry
scenes.quote: I can confirm that we, the forces of Pakistan, are already there. That I can assure you.

lines.speaker: Reporter
lines.text: Pakistan's military spokesman, Lieutenant General Ahmed Sharif Chaudhry, confirmed the deployment in an interview with CNN.

lines.speaker: Reporter
lines.text: I can confirm that we, the forces of Pakistan, *are already there*, he said, serving in multiple capabilities and domains.

lines.speaker: Reporter
lines.text: Reuters reported earlier this year that Pakistan had deployed some *eight thousand troops*, a squadron of fighter jets and an air defense system to the kingdom.

scenes.name: Sajjad Haider Khan
scenes.quote: Already we have substantial number of forces as well as resources in town, in Riyadh.

lines.speaker: Reporter
lines.text: On Friday, Pakistan's foreign ministry said it has a *substantial* number of forces and resources in Riyadh.

lines.speaker: Reporter
lines.text: But it drew a line. Pakistani troops would *not cross the border* to attack the Houthis. Their role is to defend Saudi territory.

lines.speaker: Reporter
lines.text: Pakistan has trained and advised the Saudi military for decades, while Riyadh has repeatedly helped Pakistan *financially* in hard times.

lines.speaker: Reporter
lines.text: Several allies are involved, but their roles are *very different*.

lines.speaker: Reporter
lines.text: The United States remains Saudi Arabia's key missile defense supplier. In January, Washington approved a possible *nine billion dollar* sale of seven hundred thirty Patriot interceptors.

lines.speaker: Reporter
lines.text: But approval of a sale does not mean the missiles have *arrived*.

lines.speaker: Reporter
lines.text: Britain has agreed to provide *air to air refuelling* for Saudi jets, according to the Guardian.

lines.speaker: Reporter
lines.text: Pakistan has *denied* reports that its jets carried out air strikes. Whether its troops will take part in operations against the Houthis remains unclear.

lines.speaker: Reporter
lines.text: Experts point to a basic problem: *cost*.

lines.speaker: Reporter
lines.text: Using an advanced interceptor against a much cheaper drone or missile turns every attack into an *expensive exchange*.

lines.speaker: Reporter
lines.text: The Houthis don't need to match Saudi Arabia's budget. *Occasional hits* are enough to close airports and unsettle investors.

lines.speaker: Reporter
lines.text: Last month, the Houthis also seized key areas along the *Bab el-Mandeb Strait*, and a Saudi-led coalition has been trying to take them back.

lines.speaker: Reporter
lines.text: On the ground in Yemen, government forces and *UAE backed* brigades are fighting the Houthis, coordinating with Saudi air power.

lines.speaker: Reporter
lines.text: But bombing alone has limits. A U.S. campaign in 2025 destroyed Houthi command sites and weapons stores, yet Reuters later reported it had *not cut their supply lines*.

lines.speaker: Reporter
lines.text: Diplomacy is another path. In May 2025, *Oman* announced a ceasefire between the United States and the Houthis.

lines.speaker: Reporter
lines.text: Iran also has influence over the Houthis, though experts say influence is *not the same as control*.

lines.speaker: Reporter
lines.text: India and Australia have condemned the attacks on Saudi Arabia. The Houthis, meanwhile, accuse the Saudis of striking the airport in *Sanaa*, Yemen's rebel held capital.

lines.speaker: Anchor
lines.text: So could this war pull in *the United States* as well?

scenes.name: Mohammed bin Salman
scenes.quote: Seeking help from allies. Trump weighing joining the fight against the Houthis.

lines.speaker: Reporter
lines.text: Saudi Crown Prince *Mohammed bin Salman* has been seeking assistance.

lines.speaker: Reporter
lines.text: President Trump says he is weighing *joining the fight* against the Houthis, and planned to speak with the crown prince.

lines.speaker: Reporter
lines.text: But a U.S. intervention could prompt the Houthis to halt shipping through the *Bab el-Mandeb Strait*, at the southern end of the Red Sea.

lines.speaker: Reporter
lines.text: That route has become a crucial alternative to the *Strait of Hormuz*, already threatened by Iran.

scenes.name: Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman
scenes.quote: There is no way that somebody will break our back. We are like a phoenix.

lines.speaker: Reporter
lines.text: Sunday's attack came as Riyadh hosted a major *international energy conference*.

lines.speaker: Reporter
lines.text: Saudi Energy Minister Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman struck a defiant tone. There is no way that somebody will *break our back*, he said. We are like a phoenix.

lines.speaker: Reporter
lines.text: For a kingdom trying to open up to tourism and investment, the attacks are a *serious threat*. Reporting for KOWEN News.

lines.speaker: Anchor
lines.text: To recap tonight's top story.

lines.speaker: Anchor
lines.text: A Houthi missile strike on Riyadh's airport has killed *thirteen people*, the deadliest attack on a Gulf state since the Iran war began.

lines.speaker: Anchor
lines.text: Saudi Arabia is reportedly *running low* on interceptors, and has asked France, Britain, Pakistan and Egypt for help.

lines.speaker: Anchor
lines.text: Pakistan confirms its forces are *already in the kingdom*, under a new mutual defense pact.

lines.speaker: Anchor
lines.text: And President Trump says he is weighing whether to *join the fight* against the Houthis.

lines.speaker: Anchor
lines.text: Allies are sending help, but no one can produce interceptors *overnight*.

lines.speaker: Anchor
lines.text: We'll keep following this story. That's all for tonight. This has been KOWEN News. Thanks for watching, and good night.
